lessons.title: 1 · Read a notice without adding assumptions
lessons.goal: Find who, what, where and when; distinguish a general instruction from a conditional request; identify missing information.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil, or this app's response fields. Read the fictional source aloud with a partner if helpful. This is supported comprehension and writing practice, not a beginning phonics course or a reading-level assessment.
paragraphs:
BEFORE YOU READ
Think of a notice that left you uncertain. Was a time, place, condition or contact missing? A notice helps a reader act, so a useful reading question is: 'What would I actually need to know before taking part?' This lesson uses a fictional reading-table notice, not a real event.

A REPEATABLE READING ROUTINE
First read the whole notice to learn its purpose. Next, locate the detail that answers your question. Then read the sentence around that detail, because a word such as 'if', 'before' or 'only' can change who must act. Finally, separate what the text states from what you would still need to ask. Do not fill a missing detail with a convenient guess.

WORKED EXAMPLE · A CONDITION HAS A SCOPE
Mini-notice: 'The sketch group meets on Tuesday at 4 p.m. If you need a pencil, tell Lee by Monday.'
Question: Does everyone have to contact Lee?
Thinking: The first sentence applies to the group meeting. The second begins with 'if' and names only people who need a pencil. So the text does not require every participant to contact Lee.
Useful explanation: 'Only people requesting a pencil are told to contact Lee; the condition is needing a pencil.'

WORKED EXAMPLE · A NUMBER CAN ANSWER THE WRONG QUESTION
Mini-notice: 'The room has twenty seats.' This tells the room's stated seat count. It does not tell how many people will come. Saying 'twenty people will attend' turns a capacity detail into an unsupported prediction. Ask whether the number measures what your question asks about.

PRACTICE WITH EVIDENCE
Read the source below. Line labels such as N1 are location aids, not rankings of importance. In Practice & explain, select a choice, then write which line supports it. The Passage / model tab keeps the notice available while you write. You can also write 'the sentence beginning…' rather than using a line label. Checking a choice does not grade the written explanation.

BUILD A USEFUL REPLY
A reply should preserve the stated time and place, explain any condition relevant to the reader, and label unresolved questions. Avoid adding reassurance about services the notice does not mention. A question such as 'Is there a step-free route to Room 2?' keeps missing information visible instead of treating silence as confirmation.

REVISIT
Use another ordinary, non-urgent notice later. Make two short lists: 'stated' and 'not stated'. Ask someone else to locate the supporting sentences. If they cannot find your detail in the notice, decide whether it is an inference, outside knowledge or a mistake. This practice does not establish independent reading ability.

PRACTICE SOURCE TEXT
READING TABLE — FICTIONAL PRACTICE NOTICE
[N1] The reading table meets on Saturday from 2:00 to 3:00 p.m. in Room 2.
[N2] Bring one book to discuss. You may borrow a book at the table; you do not need to own one.
[N3] No ticket or payment is needed. Room 2 has twelve chairs.
[N4] If you want a large-print reading sheet, tell Jo by Friday at noon. Jo needs time to prepare those sheets.
[N5] An older poster listed the library hall and a 1:00 p.m. start. This notice replaces that poster: use Room 2 and the 2:00 p.m. start.
[N6] The notice gives no information about transport or step-free access. Ask the organizer rather than assuming those arrangements exist.
Word help: 'large-print' means text printed in larger letters; 'replaces' means to use this notice instead of the older one for the stated details.

questions.prompt: According to the replacement notice, where does the group meet?
questions.explanation: N1 names Room 2. N5 explicitly replaces the older library-hall information. Use the location stated in the operative notice, not the superseded poster.
hints: Find the location in N1, then check the change in N5.
Which place does N5 say to use?
mistakes: A
The library hall belongs to the older poster. N5 explicitly replaces that location.
C
Jo is named as a contact for sheets. No sentence says the meeting is at Jo's home.

questions.prompt: Name one practical question the notice does not answer. Explain why guessing the answer could mislead a reader, and write a question to the organizer.
questions.explanation: Identify a genuine gap, such as transport or step-free access (N6). Distinguish it from information that is already stated. Example: 'The notice does not say whether there is a step-free route. Assuming there is one could leave someone unable to reach the room. Is there a step-free route to Room 2?' A useful answer names the gap, its consequence and a specific question. Do not invent the organizer's answer.
hints: Look at N6 for explicitly missing arrangements.
Write 'The notice does not say…' before drafting your question.

lessons.title: 2 · Trace events and support an inference
lessons.goal: Reconstruct a sequence, connect a stated cause to an event, and qualify an inference using the text.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil, or this app's response fields. Read the fictional source aloud with a partner if helpful. This is supported comprehension and writing practice, not a beginning phonics course or a reading-level assessment.
paragraphs:
BEFORE YOU READ
A story can state an action without stating every motive behind it. Keep three categories separate: a fact the narrator states, a conclusion that fits several details, and a possibility for which the text gives no evidence. All three can be discussed, but they should not be presented with the same certainty.

WORKED EXAMPLE · SEQUENCE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY CAUSE
Mini-account: 'Sam rang a bell. A cloud covered the sun.' The order tells us which event is narrated first, but it does not show that the bell caused the cloud. For a cause claim, look for a stated mechanism or other evidence linking the events. 'After' and 'because' do different jobs.

WORKED EXAMPLE · AN INFERENCE WITH A LIMIT
Mini-account: 'Ana checked both the front and back of each page before filing it.' A supported inference is that Ana was trying to avoid missing information. The account does not directly report her thoughts, so say 'This suggests… because…'. Saying 'Ana has never lost a page' reaches beyond the described action.

A SEQUENCE MAP
For each event, jot a short verb phrase: place, scatter, collect, check, recover, move. Then connect the phrases in the order the passage establishes. If a question asks for the event immediately before another event, return to the surrounding sentences; do not choose merely the most memorable action.

BUILD AN EVIDENCE SENTENCE
Use a claim, a specific detail, and a link explaining why the detail supports the claim. For example: 'The character seems concerned about completeness because she checks against a list rather than relying on memory.' The evidence is more useful than simply writing 'because the text says so'. Keep the strength of the claim proportional to the evidence.

PRACTICE
The card-box account describes one incident. Use its details to explain decisions within that incident. For the final writing task, distinguish a sensible intention from a guarantee about every future session. Ask a partner to underline your claim and circle your evidence; revise if they cannot identify both.

PRACTICE SOURCE TEXT
THE CARD BOX — FICTIONAL PRACTICE ACCOUNT
[E1] Before the reading session, Mira arranged story cards in a shallow box beside an open window.
[E2] A gust lifted the top cards onto the floor. Mira closed the window and gathered the cards.
[E3] She could not remember their original order. She checked the numbered list taped inside the lid and put the cards back in that order.
[E4] Theo suggested writing a new story immediately. Mira said, 'First I want to check that every numbered card is back.'
[E5] After checking the list, Mira found one number missing. She looked under the table and found that card.
[E6] She moved the closed box to a shelf away from the window. The account does not describe what happened at any later session.
Word help: a 'gust' is a brief strong movement of air; 'original order' means the sequence before the cards scattered.

questions.prompt: What directly scattered the top cards in the account?
questions.explanation: E2 explicitly links the gust to the cards lifting onto the floor. The other actions do not explain that event in the account.
hints: Look for the sentence in which the scattering actually happens.
E2 names what lifted the cards.
mistakes: A
Theo only suggests a new story later, in E4. That suggestion did not scatter the cards.
B
The list is checked after the cards have scattered, to restore their order.

Read what happened just before that action.

lessons.title: 3 · Summarize a report and keep its limits
lessons.goal: Identify a report's main point, select relevant evidence, and write a summary without inventing findings.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil, or this app's response fields. Read the fictional source aloud with a partner if helpful. This is supported comprehension and writing practice, not a beginning phonics course or a reading-level assessment.
paragraphs:
BEFORE YOU READ
A summary helps another reader understand the main point without reading every detail. Shortness alone is not enough: a short statement can still distort the source. Ask what the text is chiefly explaining, what evidence matters to that explanation, and what limitation would change the reader's interpretation if omitted.

WORKED EXAMPLE · DETAIL VERSUS MAIN POINT
Mini-report: 'A club moved its pencils from three drawers to one labeled tray. Members then found the pencils in that tray during two meetings. The club has not tracked whether this arrangement remains useful over a term.'
Too narrow: 'The club had three drawers.'
Too strong: 'The tray permanently solved every storage problem.'
Better: 'A labeled tray helped members locate pencils during two meetings, but longer-term usefulness has not been checked.'

BUILD A THREE-PART NOTE
Write one phrase each for purpose, observed result, and limit. Then combine the phrases into sentences. Keep verbs accurate: 'reported', 'observed', 'suggested' and 'proved' make different claims. Do not replace a limited observation with an assertion about every person or every situation.

WORKED REVISION · REMOVE AN INVENTED MEASUREMENT
Draft: 'Everyone found pencils twice as fast.'
Check against the mini-report: no times were recorded, not every person is described, and 'twice' has no numerical support.
Revision: 'Members found the pencils in the labeled tray during the two meetings described.'
Reason: the revised sentence reports what was observed without supplying a measurement the source never made.

CHOOSING WHAT TO KEEP
A fact may be true but irrelevant to a particular summary. A box's decorative color would not normally explain how an instruction changed, unless the report connected color to the result. Conversely, a limitation about who took part may matter if the summary otherwise sounds like a controlled comparison. Relevance depends on the question you are answering.

PRACTICE
Read the label trial as a report of a small fictional session. Its numerical counts are real within the exercise, but they do not turn it into evidence about all learners. Write a summary that allows a reader to distinguish the observed question pattern from the group's next decision and from things the group did not measure.

PRACTICE SOURCE TEXT
THE LABEL TRIAL — FICTIONAL PRACTICE REPORT
[R1] A reading group compared two labels for its story-card boxes. The old label said 'Cards'. The trial label said 'Story cards: match the number on each card to the list in the lid'.
[R2] Four volunteers each sorted one practice set. Two used the old label; two different volunteers used the trial label. The sets contained the same number of cards.
[R3] Both old-label volunteers asked where the order was recorded. Neither trial-label volunteer asked that question during this session.
[R4] The group did not record sorting times or test another session. It also did not check whether the two pairs had equal prior experience.
[R5] The group kept the clearer wording for its next session and planned to observe whether further questions arose.
Word help: 'trial' means a test use; 'prior experience' means what someone had done before this session. These are invented observations, not research findings.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the report's main point?
choices: A clearer label was tried; this session showed a different question pattern, with important limits.
Story cards must always have four labels.
The report mainly explains how fast every volunteer sorted.
questions.explanation: R1–R3 describe a label comparison and a question pattern; R4 states limits; R5 describes the next step. Option A includes that central relationship without inventing a universal rule or timing result.
hints: Read the purpose in R1, result in R3 and limits in R4 together.
Choose a statement broad enough to cover the report but no broader than its evidence.
mistakes: B
Four counts the volunteers in R2. It is not a required number of labels.
C
R4 explicitly says sorting times were not recorded. A timing claim cannot be the report's supported main finding.

Because the trial label had no words.

questions.explanation: R2 uses different volunteers for the labels, and R4 says prior experience was not checked. The observed difference could have more than one explanation; the report does not isolate the label's effect.
hints: Compare the volunteers described in R2 with the missing check in R4.
Was the label the only possible relevant difference between the pairs?
mistakes: A
Observations can be reported accurately. The issue is moving from an observed difference to an isolated cause without enough support.
B
R1 quotes the trial label's wording. This option contradicts the source.

questions.prompt: Write a two- or three-sentence summary that includes the label change, the observed question pattern, and one important limitation.
questions.explanation: Check: identify the added instruction about matching numbers to the lid list; report that both old-label volunteers asked about order and neither trial-label volunteer did in this session; retain a limitation such as different people/unchecked prior experience or no repeat session. Example: 'The group tried a label explaining where to find the card order. Both old-label volunteers asked about order, while neither trial-label volunteer did during this session. Different volunteers used the labels and their prior experience was not checked, so the label's effect was not isolated.' Equivalent wording is valid. Remove claims about speed or all learners.
hints: Make three notes: change, observed result, limit.

lessons.title: 4 · Turn a vague draft into usable instructions
lessons.goal: Name objects clearly, order dependent actions, and include a check tied to the required result.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil, or this app's response fields. Read the fictional source aloud with a partner if helpful. This is supported comprehension and writing practice, not a beginning phonics course or a reading-level assessment.
paragraphs:
BEFORE YOU WRITE
An instruction can sound familiar to its author while leaving a new reader unsure what to do. Decide who will use it and what a finished result must contain. In this lesson the result is a harmless paper packet. A reader should be able to check the packet against the requirement, not merely decide that it looks tidy.

WORKED EXAMPLE · REPLACE AN UNCLEAR PRONOUN
Draft: 'Put the list beside the folder, then label it.' The word 'it' could mean the list or the folder.
Revision, if the folder is the intended object: 'Put the list beside the folder. Write the project name on the folder.'
Reason: the noun resolves the ambiguity. If the author does not know which object was intended, ask; grammatical tidying cannot supply a missing requirement.

WORKED EXAMPLE · PUT A CHECK WHERE IT CAN HELP
Suppose a packet must contain three colored paper slips. A useful sequence is: select one of each required color, compare the selection with the requirement, place the slips in the packet, and label it. 'Check everything at some point' does not tell a reader what to compare or when to do it. The check should identify missing or duplicated contents while they can still be corrected easily.

FROM REQUIREMENT TO STEPS
Underline the required objects, quantities, order and label. Make a numbered list with a clear action verb at the beginning of each step. Keep two actions together only if their relationship remains easy to follow. Replace 'there', 'it' and 'them' when more than one object could fit. Do not add details merely to make the list longer.

A CHECK IS MORE THAN 'BE CAREFUL'
A useful completion check compares the result with something definite. For example, 'Match each selected slip to the three colors named in the requirement; there must be one of each' is testable. 'Make it nice' leaves the criterion undefined. When a requirement is incomplete, record the missing decision instead of inventing one silently.

TEST THE WORDING
Read your instructions aloud or ask another person to act them out with paper. Observe where they pause or ask a question. Record the exact phrase that caused trouble and revise it. One successful trial gives useful feedback about that trial; it is not proof that the instructions will work for every reader. Practice includes both choosing revisions and writing your own complete sequence.

PRACTICE SOURCE TEXT
MAKING A STORY-CARD PACKET — FICTIONAL PRACTICE MODEL
[I1] Required result: one packet containing cards numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4, with each number present once. Card 1 should be on top. The envelope label should say 'River story — cards 1–4'. Use only paper cards and an envelope.
[I2] Draft instructions: 'Put them in order and put it in there. Check it. Write the name.'
[I3] Available materials: one envelope; cards marked 1, 2, 3, 3 and 4; a pencil. The extra card 3 is a duplicate and should be set aside, not packed.
[I4] A previous reader put the envelope away before checking the cards, then had to reopen it to remove a duplicate. This is one reader's experience, not proof that every reader would do the same.
[I5] Revision goal: make the objects, order of actions and completion check explicit. Do not invent a new story title or change the required contents.
Word help: 'duplicate' means an extra copy of something already present; 'explicit' means directly stated rather than left for the reader to guess.

questions.prompt: Which replacement best resolves the vague objects in 'put it in there' for this packet?
choices: Put it in the correct place.

questions.explanation: The revised sentence names the cards, the destination and the required top card from I1. It gives the reader concrete referents rather than substituting another vague location.
hints: Identify the object being moved and its destination in I1.
A useful revision also preserves the required order.
mistakes: A
'It' and 'the correct place' still leave the object and destination unspecified.
C
'Anywhere nearby' contradicts the specified envelope destination and does not preserve the required order.

lessons.title: 5 · Revise a request against its evidence
lessons.goal: Plan and revise a practical message with a clear request, supported details, an appropriate limit and a next step.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil, or this app's response fields. Read the fictional source aloud with a partner if helpful. This is supported comprehension and writing practice, not a beginning phonics course or a reading-level assessment.
paragraphs:
START WITH THE READER'S TASK
Before writing, complete this sentence: 'After reading my message, I want the reader to…'. A request should make that action easy to identify. Then list the facts the reader needs, the facts you know, and the decisions still open. This separates planning the message from polishing its punctuation.

WORKED EXAMPLE · PLAN A DIFFERENT REQUEST
Brief: a group needs three folders on Monday to hold its existing notes; availability is unknown.
Plan: ask for three folders; explain the note-storage purpose; state Monday; ask what is available.
Draft: 'Could you provide three folders by Monday for our existing group notes? Please let us know whether they are available; if fewer are available, tell us how many so we can adjust.'
Why it works: the quantity, purpose and timing are concrete, while the unconfirmed supply remains a question.

WORKED REVISION · REMOVE UNSUPPORTED PRESSURE
Draft: 'Everybody demands these folders now.' The brief did not mention everybody's views or an immediate deadline. A courteous revision can be precise without inventing urgency: 'Could you provide three folders by Monday?' Tone does not excuse changing the facts, and a polite sentence can still be misleading if its quantity or date is wrong.

REVISION PASSES
First revise meaning: is the requested action clear, and are quantities, dates and evidence accurate? Next revise organization: put the request where the reader can find it, group its purpose with it, and finish with a useful reply or next step. Finally edit sentences and punctuation. Fixing spelling alone will not repair a wrong quantity or an unsupported guarantee.

USE FEEDBACK AS A QUESTION
Instead of 'This is unclear', try 'Which materials are requested?' or 'Does this date mean today or the meeting day?' Read the answer from the draft itself. If you have to rely on the writer's spoken explanation, add the needed information to the message. Preserve the reader's question in your notes so you can check the revision against it.

FINAL PRACTICE AND TRANSFER
The source contains a brief and an intentionally flawed draft. Compare every claim in the draft with the brief. Write your own message, then explain one revision and the evidence behind it. Later, use the same routine with a different fictional request. A checked choice is useful practice, but the quality of a whole message still needs human reading and discussion.

PRACTICE SOURCE TEXT
REQUEST FOR READING MATERIALS — FICTIONAL PRACTICE BRIEF
[W1] Purpose: ask the group coordinator for six reusable blank reading cards before Thursday's planning meeting. The cards will be used to draft discussion prompts.
[W2] Known facts: the group currently has two blank cards. The planning activity calls for eight blank cards in total. The coordinator has not confirmed whether six more are available.
[W3] If six cards are unavailable, ask the coordinator how many can be supplied; the group will then adjust the activity. No money, attendance count or urgent deadline beyond the planning meeting is specified.
[W4] Draft message: 'We urgently need loads of things. Everyone is waiting. Send eight new cards tomorrow because the plan is guaranteed to work. Thanks.'
[W5] Revision goal: make a clear, courteous request that preserves the known quantity, purpose and timing, and asks about availability without claiming it is confirmed.
Word help: 'coordinator' means the person organizing the group's materials; 'confirmed' means explicitly established, not merely hoped for. The people and arrangements are fictional.

questions.prompt: Which requested quantity follows the brief?
questions.explanation: W1 explicitly requests six cards. W2 explains why: eight are needed in total and two are already available, leaving six additional cards. Total required and additional requested are different quantities.
hints: Separate the total needed from what the group already has.
Check W1 against the 8-total and 2-existing facts in W2.
mistakes: A
Eight is the total required, not the additional request. Two cards already exist.
B
The brief provides a precise quantity. 'Loads' makes the coordinator guess what to supply.
